name: Erysipelas

likely: Other beta-hemolytic streptococci (groups B, C, G)
pathogens.why: Erysipelas is distinguished from cellulitis precisely because its sharply demarcated, raised border reflects involvement limited to the superficial dermis and lymphatics, a pattern essentially always caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci rather than the broader organism range seen in deeper cellulitis.

investigations.why: Diagnosis is clinical based on the characteristic appearance; cultures of intact skin have low yield.
May identify bacteremic spread in more severe presentations.

references: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines
reason: Sharply demarcated, raised erythema (the hallmark distinguishing erysipelas from the less well-defined borders of cellulitis) with systemic symptoms indicates a superficial dermal/lymphatic infection, almost always streptococcal. Narrow-spectrum penicillin-based therapy is appropriate given the high reliability of streptococcal etiology in this specific presentation.

clinicalPearls: Abrupt onset of fiery-red swelling of the face or extremities, with well-defined indurated margins (notably along the nasolabial fold), rapid progression, and intense pain (Harrison 22e p.1052).

The sharply demarcated, raised border distinguishes erysipelas from cellulitis and reflects involvement limited to the superficial (upper) dermis and superficial lymphatics rather than the deeper subcutaneous tissue (Harrison 22e p.1051, p.1210).
A peau d'orange (orange-peel) texture of the skin is characteristic and is thought to reflect involvement of superficial lymphatics (Harrison 22e p.1210).
Lesion typically develops over a few hours and is accompanied by fever and chills; flaccid superficial blebs/bullae may appear on the second or third day (Harrison 22e p.1052, p.1210).
Classic distribution is the malar area of the face (often extending over the bridge of the nose to the contralateral malar region) or the lower extremities (Harrison 22e p.1210).
Infants and elderly adults are most commonly affected, and the severity of systemic toxicity varies (Harrison 22e p.1052).
Desquamation of the involved skin occurs roughly 5-10 days into the illness (Harrison 22e p.1052).
Classic cases with typical features are almost always due to beta-hemolytic streptococci, usually group A and occasionally group C or G (Harrison 22e p.1210).
harrison.pathophysiology: Streptococcus pyogenes infecting the epidermis is translocated laterally to deeper structures via lymphatics, producing the characteristic rapid superficial spread of erysipelas. Subsequent engorgement or obstruction of lymphatics causes flaccid edema of the epidermis. The infection is confined to the superficial dermis and superficial lymphatics (in contrast to cellulitis, which involves deeper subcutaneous tissue), and extension to deeper soft tissues is rare (Harrison 22e p.1051-1052, p.1210).
infectionMimics: Cellulitis (deeper dermal/subcutaneous involvement, with less sharply demarcated borders) (Harrison 22e p.1210)

Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis, which can produce a similar appearance, especially when the lesion is atypical, less intensely red, fades into surrounding skin, or arises around a wound or ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1210-1211)
redFlags: Edema with purple bullae, ecchymosis, and cutaneous anesthesia suggests loss of vascular integrity and necessitates exploration of deeper structures for necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1051).
Unexplained fever with disproportionate pain and tenderness in soft tissue, even without acute cutaneous inflammation, should raise suspicion for a deeper necrotizing process (Harrison 22e p.1051).
harrison.prognosis: Generally responds well to therapy; with appropriate treatment, fever, pain, and the intense red color diminish, although swelling may continue to progress initially. Recurrence at the same site (sometimes years later) is not uncommon, particularly where normal lymphatic drainage has been disrupted (Harrison 22e p.1052, p.1210-1211).
pitfalls: Atypical erysipelas may involve an unusual anatomic site, appear less intensely red, fade into surrounding skin, or cause only mild systemic illness, in which case a specific clinical diagnosis cannot reliably be made and broader empirical coverage (including S. aureus) is prudent (Harrison 22e p.1210-1211).
Extension to deeper soft tissues is rare in true erysipelas; if present, reconsider the diagnosis and exclude a deeper or necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1052).

In most parts of the world, acute rheumatic fever is NOT a sequela of streptococcal skin infection (unlike pharyngitis), though post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis may follow either skin or throat infection (Harrison 22e p.1210).
